title: Mechanics and Terminology of Accounting
tagline: Why businesses keep accounts, what debit and credit mean, and the ten accounting terms the syllabus prescribes — understood, not calculated.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Commercial Applications syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by AglaSem, Scribd and Oswal Publishers; cisce.org returned 403). No board examination paper was consulted, every question is original practice, no figure is presented as an official statistic, and — as the syllabus itself requires — no question asks the student to record accounting entries or perform accounting calculations.

overview.intro: Unit 4(a)–(c) opens the accounting half of the syllabus with understanding firmly in charge: the need and relevance of accounting, a basic understanding of debit and credit, and the basic terminology — capital, liability, asset, revenue, expense, purchase, sales, stocks, debtors and creditors. The syllabus states explicitly that no questions will be set on recording entries or calculations, so this chapter teaches meaning, not mechanics of bookkeeping: what each term denotes, how the terms relate, and how a student should think about a transaction before any figure is involved. That constraint is itself examinable and is treated as such throughout.

learningOutcomes: State the need and relevance of accounting for a business.
Explain what debit and credit mean in an account.
Define each of the ten prescribed accounting terms with an example.
Classify given items as assets, liabilities, capital, revenue or expense.
Explain the accounting equation and where a transaction affects it.

learn.title: The need and relevance of accounting

blocks.text: Accounting is the process of identifying, recording and summarising the financial transactions of a business so that interested parties can judge how it is doing. A business that does not keep accounts is flying blind: it cannot tell whether it earned or lost, what it owns against what it owes, or whether it can pay wages next month. Four needs follow directly. Measurement of profit or loss — revenue earned against expense incurred shows whether the business worked. Statement of financial position — what the firm owns and what it owes to outsiders tells the owner the net stake. Decision-making — records of cost, sales and stock guide pricing and purchasing. Compliance and trust — the law, tax authorities, banks and investors all require accounts because none of them will rely on memory. Relevance grows with size: a street vendor can hold the whole business in mind, but a firm with employees, credit and stock in a warehouse cannot, and the moment transactions become too numerous to remember, accounting becomes the firm’s memory. The syllabus places this chapter first because every later record — journal, ledger, cash book, trial balance — exists to serve these needs.

blocks.caption: The four needs accounting serves
rows: Did the business earn in this period?
What is owned and what is owed?
Which product, supplier or price works?
Can the transactions be shown and verified?

learn.title: Debit and credit: the two sides of every account

blocks.text: Every account has two sides, and debit and credit are simply their names — debit comes from the left, credit from the right, and every transaction touches both sides so that the accounts always balance. The working understanding the syllabus asks for is this: an account is debited when something is received by it and credited when something is given by it. When goods are bought, the supplier’s account receives the obligation and the purchase is recorded as a debit; when a debtor pays, cash receives the amount and the debtor’s account is credited because the claim has been given up. Two consequences matter for exam answers. Debit does not mean good and credit does not mean bad — the words carry no praise or blame, only direction. And because every transaction has two equal sides, total debits always equal total credits, which is the property that lets an accountant later detect errors by comparing the two totals. The syllabus asks for a basic understanding, so the marks lie in stating the direction rule and applying it to a described transaction, never in preparing an entry — which the syllabus expressly excludes.

items: Debit = left side = the account receiving; credit = right side = the account giving.
Every transaction is recorded on both sides, so total debits equal total credits.
Neither term carries a positive or negative judgement; both are directions.
The syllabus excludes recording entries and calculations — understanding the direction is what is examined.

blocks.text: The syllabus names ten terms, and each definition should carry meaning plus one example. Capital is the money the owner invests in the business — the owner’s claim on the firm. An asset is what the business owns or is owed that will benefit it in future: cash, machinery, buildings, stock and money owed by customers. A liability is what the business owes to outsiders: money to suppliers, loans and unpaid expenses. Revenue is the income earned from the firm’s normal activity — the price received for goods sold or services rendered. Expense is the cost incurred to earn that revenue: rent, wages, electricity, carriage. Purchase means buying goods of the kind the firm sells, so a textile mill buying yarn is a purchase while buying a delivery van is not. Sales means selling those goods in the course of trade. Stocks are the goods lying unsold at a given date — opening stock brought forward and closing stock held at the end. Debtors are persons or firms who owe the business money for goods sold on credit. Creditors are persons or firms the business owes money to for goods bought on credit. The pairing is where students slip: debtors are owed to you, creditors are owed by you, and purchase and sales refer only to goods dealt in, not to any buy or any sell.

learn.title: Relating the terms: ownership, obligation and the equation

blocks.text: The ten terms are not a list but a structure, held together by one relationship: everything the business owns is financed either by the owner or by outsiders. Written as the accounting equation, assets equal capital plus liabilities — the machinery and stock came from the proprietor’s investment and from what the firm borrowed. Classification questions are then answered by asking what each item is. Cash, stock, debtors and fixed assets are assets because they belong to or are owed to the business. Loans, creditors and unpaid expenses are liabilities because outsiders can claim them. Capital belongs to the owner’s side. Revenue and expense are the two flows that move the owner’s side over time: revenue increases capital and expense reduces it, which is why profit is capital grown and loss is capital shrunk. Purchase and sales are specific transactions within those flows — purchases reduce cash or create creditors, sales create revenue and often debtors. Hold the equation while reading any transaction and the direction becomes obvious: if the firm receives an asset while a liability rises equally, the equation stays balanced, which is the check that confirms debit and credit are working. This is the whole of the understanding the syllabus requires; figures and entries are expressly outside it.

blocks.caption: Where each term sits in the accounting equation
rows: Grows by profit, falls by loss
Rise with credit purchases, fall on payment

items.text: The owner adds a delivery van worth a stated sum to the business.
items.note: Asset rises and capital rises by the same amount — the equation stays balanced.

items.note: Stock rises and a liability to the creditor rises equally — nothing else moves.

keyPoints: Accounting records transactions so that profit, position, decisions and compliance can be supported.
Debit is the receiving side and credit the giving side; both apply to every transaction.
Debit and credit carry no positive or negative meaning — only direction.
Total debits equal total credits, which is how errors are detected later.
Assets are what the business owns or is owed; liabilities are what it owes outsiders.
Capital is the owner’s claim; it grows with profit and falls with loss.
Revenue is income from normal activity; expense is the cost of earning it.
Purchase and sales refer only to goods the firm deals in, not to every buy and sell.
Debtors owe the business; creditors are owed by the business.
The equation Assets = Capital + Liabilities keeps every transaction in balance.
The syllabus forbids questions on recording entries or calculations — meaning only.
examFocus: “What is the need for accounting?” — four needs with the user who relies on each.
“Explain debit and credit” — direction rule, two-sided effect, balance property, and a described transaction; no entries.
“Define asset and liability with examples” — definition, two examples, and the statement that they sit on opposite sides of the equation.

options: The side of an account that receives
A payment made to a creditor
questions.answer: The side of an account that receives
questions.explanation: Debit names the left-hand, receiving side of an account; it carries no judgement about whether the transaction is good or bad.
questions.commonMistake: Debit does not mean expense — direction and type of transaction are different questions.

questions.prompt: A textile mill buys yarn to manufacture cloth. This is recorded as:
questions.explanation: Purchase means buying goods of the kind the business deals in; yarn is the mill’s trading material, so the transaction is a purchase rather than a general expense.
questions.commonMistake: Buying a delivery van would not be a purchase, because the mill does not deal in vans.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a liability of the business?
options: Money owed to a supplier for goods bought on credit
questions.answer: Money owed to a supplier for goods bought on credit
questions.explanation: A liability is an amount owed to an outsider; the supplier is a creditor and can claim payment, whereas machinery, cash and stock are assets the firm holds.
questions.commonMistake: Stock is an asset even though it will be paid for — the obligation to pay is the liability.

questions.prompt: The effect of incurring an expense on the accounting equation is to:
options: Reduce capital, with assets falling or a liability rising by the same amount
Increase liabilities without any other change
questions.answer: Reduce capital, with assets falling or a liability rising by the same amount
questions.explanation: Expense is the cost of earning revenue and it reduces the owner’s claim; the other side is either cash paid out or an amount now owed, so the equation remains balanced.
questions.commonMistake: Expense never raises capital — revenue does that.

questions.prompt: The accounting equation is Assets = ______ + Liabilities.
questions.explanation: Everything the business owns is financed either by the owner, whose claim is capital, or by outsiders, whose claims are liabilities.
questions.commonMistake: Do not write “profit” — profit is a change in capital, not a side of the equation.

questions.prompt: State the need for accounting in a business under any three heads.
questions.answer: To ascertain profit or loss — revenue against expense shows whether the period worked. To state the financial position — what is owned against what is owed shows the owner’s net stake. To aid decision-making — records of cost, sales and stock guide pricing, purchasing and staffing. It also satisfies the requirements of law, tax authorities and banks, who will not accept memory as evidence.
questions.explanation: Each head names the need and the user it serves, which is why accounting is called the language of business.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer “to pay tax” alone; tax is one user of accounts, not the whole purpose.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a debtor and a creditor with an example of each.
questions.answer: A debtor is a person or firm that owes the business money, usually for goods sold on credit — for example, a shop that took cloth on credit and must pay for it. A creditor is a person or firm to whom the business owes money, usually for goods bought on credit — for example, the yarn supplier waiting for payment. A debtor is an asset of the business because the amount will be received; a creditor is a liability because the amount must be paid.
questions.explanation: The direction of the obligation is the distinguishing feature, and classifying each as asset or liability completes the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Do not distinguish them by who they are — the same firm can be both, depending on the transaction.

questions.prompt: Define asset, liability and capital, and explain how they are related through the accounting equation.
questions.answer: An asset is something the business owns or is owed that will benefit it in future, such as cash, machinery, buildings, stock and amounts due from customers. A liability is an amount the business owes to outsiders, such as money due to suppliers, loans and unpaid expenses. Capital is the owner’s investment in the business — the owner’s claim on the business’s assets. The three are related by the accounting equation: assets equal capital plus liabilities, because everything the business holds was financed either by the owner or by people who lent to it. The equation also acts as a check on every transaction — when goods are bought on credit, stock, an asset, rises and the liability to the supplier rises equally, so the equation stays balanced. If profit is earned, capital rises and assets rise with it; if a loss is incurred, capital falls. The relationship therefore explains where every item belongs and why the accounts must balance.
questions.explanation: Each term is defined with examples and then connected through the equation, with a transaction showing that the balance is maintained — the full understanding the syllabus asks for.
questions.commonMistake: Do not define the three in isolation; the relationship is the part that earns the third mark.

questions.prompt: Explain debit and credit as the two sides of an account, and show with an example that they always balance.
questions.answer: Every account has two sides: the debit side, which is the left, and the credit side, which is the right. An account is debited when it receives and credited when it gives, so each transaction is recorded on both sides in equal amounts. Suppose a customer pays the business an amount owed for goods bought on credit: cash, which is receiving, is debited, and the customer’s account is credited because the claim against him is given up. The two effects are equal, so total debits equal total credits — the property that allows a later comparison of the two totals to reveal any error. Another example: when the owner brings capital into the business, cash receives and is debited while capital is credited with the same amount, again keeping the totals equal. Neither term implies gain or loss; they are directions, and their equality is what keeps the accounts balanced.
questions.explanation: The direction rule is stated, two examples show both sides being recorded, and the equality of the totals is drawn out as the consequence — exactly the basic understanding the syllabus prescribes.
questions.commonMistake: The syllabus excludes recording entries, so describe the direction of the effect instead of writing a journal entry.

questions.prompt: Classify each of the following as asset, liability, capital, revenue or expense, justifying each classification: a delivery van owned by the firm; an amount due from a customer; a loan from a bank; the price received for goods sold; rent paid for the shop; and the money the proprietor originally invested. State what the question does not ask you to do, with the syllabus reason.
questions.answer: The delivery van is an asset, because the firm owns it and it will serve the business in future. The amount due from a customer is an asset, because it is owed to the business and will be received. The loan from a bank is a liability, because it is an amount owed to an outsider who can claim repayment. The price received for goods sold is revenue, because it is income from the firm’s ordinary activity of dealing in those goods. Rent paid for the shop is an expense, because it is a cost incurred to earn that revenue and it reduces capital. The proprietor’s original investment is capital, because it is the owner’s claim on the business. What the question does not ask for is a journal entry, a ledger account or any calculation of totals: the syllabus states that no questions will be set on recording accounting entries or calculations, and that only a basic understanding of debit, credit and the terminology is required. The classifications therefore stand on meaning — what each item is and which side of the equation it occupies — and that is the whole of the requirement.
questions.explanation: Each item is classified with the reason it belongs there, and the closing paragraph states the syllabus’s express exclusion, showing that the candidate knows the boundary of the unit as well as its content.
questions.commonMistake: Attempting a journal entry here wastes time and answers a question the syllabus says will not be set.
